subject: Chemistry
title: Gay-Lussac's Law of Combining Volumes
description: One-minute skill: Gay-Lussac's Law of Combining Volumes.

hook.text: Joseph Gay-Lussac discovered that gases combine in simple whole-number volume ratios. This puzzled everyone.

buildup.text: Two volumes of hydrogen combine with one volume of oxygen to make two volumes of water vapor. Always 2:1:2.

discovery.text: Simple ratios suggested that gases contain equal numbers of particles in equal volumes—but Dalton disagreed.

twist.text: Dalton couldn't accept that some elements existed as two-atom molecules (H₂, O₂). He thought atoms were always single.

climax.text: Avogadro solved it: gases form diatomic molecules. Two hydrogen molecules plus one oxygen molecule makes two water molecules.

punchline.text: Simple volume ratios, diatomic molecules. Gases were counting atoms for us.

quiz.question: What did Gay-Lussac's law reveal about how gases combine?
options: They react in simple whole-number volume ratios
Heavier gases always sink below lighter gases

details.summary: In 1808 Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac demonstrated that gases combine in simple whole-number volume ratios at constant temperature and pressure. This law provided crucial experimental support for atomic theory and hinted that equal volumes contain equal numbers of particles.
details.whyItMatters: Gay-Lussac's volumetric data bridged the gap between Dalton's atomic weights and Avogadro's molecular hypothesis, laying groundwork for modern gas chemistry.
takeaways: Gases react in simple whole-number volume ratios
This law supported Dalton's idea of fixed atomic proportions
It helped Avogadro propose his equal-volumes hypothesis

faq.question: What is an example of Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes?
faq.answer: Two volumes of hydrogen gas combine with one volume of oxygen gas to produce two volumes of water vapor. The ratio is exactly 2:1:2, demonstrating the simple whole-number relationship Gay-Lussac observed across many gas reactions.

faq.question: Why did Dalton initially reject Gay-Lussac's findings?
faq.answer: Dalton believed atoms could not be split and struggled with the idea that one volume of oxygen could produce two volumes of water vapor. Accepting Gay-Lussac's data required the concept of diatomic molecules, which Dalton resisted until Avogadro's later clarification.
